newsitem.title: USA: Automakers seen keeping '98 price hikes modest.
newsitem.headline: Automakers seen keeping '98 price hikes modest.

text.p: Thinking about a new car? It may pay to wait a few months.
The same balky buyers who have driven up incentives and softened sales this year are forcing automakers to take a hard look at prices for the upcoming 1998 model year.

Detroit's Big Three and foreign automakers are expected to dangle a variety of modest price hikes, outright cuts and enhanced equipment packages for no extra cost to lure people into showrooms, according to industry analysts.

"I would say net pricing, when it's all said and done, will be fairly modest," said Nicholas Lobaccaro, an analyst at Merrill Lynch. "There's no question there is no pricing power in this industry anymore."

For the second year in a row, analysts said they would not be surprised to see automakers continue rebates on 1998 models. Traditionally, incentives are withheld for the first few months of the new model year until inventories pile up. But Chrysler broke ranks last summer by slapping rebates on some 1997 models.

Susan Jacobs, president of the Jacobs & Associates consulting firm, said the ballooning number of used vehicles is contributing to the continuing need for rebates. At the same time, broader economic conditions remain generally upbeat.
"Even on the new products among the Big Three there may be pressure for incentives faster than most people expect," she said.

A year ago, Ford Motor Co. had the smallest average increase of the Big Three -- 1.2 percent on a comparably equipped basis. The Big Three as a group posted a combined price hike of 1.6 percent for the 1997 model year, significantly less than the 2.5 percent for the prior year.

Consumers will still not find many breaks on red-hot products like the Ford Expedition full-size sport/utility. But anecdotal signs are surfacing about what could be a dogfight in the popular mid-size and small car segments.

Officials at Saturn Corp. acknowledged this week that with no major new product upgrades, there is little room to justify price hikes. Sales at Saturn, a General Motors Corp. unit, were down 8.7 percent through the first five months of this year.
"It's a tough market. Whatever pricing we release, it's going to be competitive," said Saturn spokesman Greg Martin.
Prices for one potential Saturn competitor, the Altima from Nissan Motor Co. Ltd, were last week slashed 7.6 percent for the most popularly equipped version.
Much like Toyota Motor Corp. 's Camry did last year, the 1998 Accord from Honda Motor Co. Ltd. is expected to send a jolt through the core mid-size passenger car market.

Honda is presumed to have trimmed $1,000 to $1,500 out of the cost of the new Accord, analysts said. Those cost savings may translate into a lower entry level price and improved equipment packages for not much more money on other versions, said James Hall, vice president of industry analysis at consulting firm AutoPacific Inc.
"The effect of the Accord and Camry -- that's going to be a blood bath next year," Hall said.
GM, which is scheduled to release its 1998 model year prices on Thursday, will be the first of the major automakers to unveil its strategy.

A year ago, GM bumped up prices an average of 1.7 percent on a comparably equipped basis. At the time, GM said its modest price hikes were designed to more closely mirror what consumers actually pay and avoid cash rebates. But in the end, GM had to raise incentives anyway to keep up with competitors.

Analysts said the biggest question mark for this fall is Chrysler Corp.. The U.S. No. 3 automaker will introduce all-new versions of its Concorde and Intrepid, followed next spring by a new LHS full-size sedan.

The new cars feature racy styling, a more luxurious feel and a new family of engines. What is unclear is whether Chrysler -- which has experienced the biggest drop in Big Three sales this year -- will attach higher prices to reflect the new look and recoup investment costs.
Chrysler spokesman Mike McKesson declined to make any comments regarding the company's 1998 prices.
